parts.title: The power of music
parts.article:
The power of music
 
A Robert Matthews looks at research into the effects of music. Music is becoming ever more popular electronically. To meet our craving for music, internet sites are using increasingly sophisticated ways of putting us in touch with artists we may not even know we like. Most work by trawling our existing files or online listening habits and looking for patterns so they can recommend new artists for their subscribers to listen to. The search often turns up surprises. But is it possible to tease apart our likes and dislikes to identify precisely what it is about some music that thrills us or leaves us cold?
 
B For centuries composers have sought to create unforgettable music using accepted notions about the emotional appeal of certain combinations of sounds, yet only now are scientists starting to uncover what it is about these combinations that can have such a dramatic effect on our minds. Given that archaeologists have found musical instruments played by Neanderthals at least 50,000 years ago, why have scientists taken so long to investigate such a source of pleasure?
 
C 'For psychologists, who are always desperate to show that their work is rigorous, there's an image problem in tackling the emotionality of music,' says Professor Norman Cook of Kansai University in Osaka, Japan, one of the pioneers of the new science of music. 'Emotion is such a slippery topic.' The other problem, says Cook, is the long-standing principle among psychologists that our response to music is an acquired one, rather than something that is stimulated by the effect of sound on our brain cells. Yet one of the first insights to emerge from this new branch of psychology is that music affects our brains at a very basic level.
 
D Together with his colleague, Professor Takefumi Hayashi, Cook has been investigating one of the best-known examples of the emotional impact of music: the difference between major and minor chords. For centuries, composers have known that notes arranged to form major chords sound happy and upbeat, while those in minor chords sound mournful. In tests, even three-year-olds have been shown to link music in a major mode to happy faces and minor modes to sad faces.
 
E According to Cook, analysis of how people respond to notes suggests a link with how our brains interpret certain sounds in everyday life. He points out that sad-sounding minor chords can be formed by raising the pitch of any of a set of notes, while dropping the pitch produces a major chord. The same change in pitch works as an emotional telltale in communication between some mammals, where rising pitch is used to communicate weakness or defeat, while falling pitch signals social dominance. It's also present in our speech. 'A rising inflection is used to denote questions, politeness or deference, whereas a falling inflection signals dominance,' says Cook.
 
F This suggests that music in major and minor modes taps into some very basic features of how we relate to the world and each other – perhaps dating back millions of years. Could music in general be doing something similar? Quite possibly, according to research into how music triggers certain types of brain activity. At McGill University in Canada, Professor Robert Zatorre and his colleagues have carried out studies in which volunteers listen to different types of music while their brain activity is monitored. The biggest surprise was the evidence that pleasurable music activates brain circuitry which has been in existence in the human brain for thousands of years, says Zatorre. 'We share it with rats and other distant relatives on the evolutionary tree – and it's typically associated with biological rewards, like food, for example.'
 
G At the University of Oxford, Dr Joyce Chen has been looking into another celebrated feature of music – the irresistibility of rhythm. Her interest was sparked by studies involving patients with movement difficulties. If music that had a strong rhythm – say, a marching band – was played to these patients, they were able to improve their walking ability, says Chen. In an attempt to find out why the simple act of listening to music might help disabled patients, Dr Chen and colleagues from the International Laboratory for Brain, Music and Sound Research in Montreal carried out brain scans on volunteers who were listening to rhythmic sounds. The criteria for selecting these volunteers were that they should be in first-rate physical health but musically untrained. The results have been another revelation. Chen and her colleagues found the rhythms triggered activity in parts of the brain linked to hearing, but something even more surprising was that the rhythms also triggered activity in the motor regions of the brain, linked to active movement.
 
H 'Somehow, the mere act of just listening triggers motor-neural activity. Maybe this is one reason why we often tap our feet, move or dance when hearing music,' says Chen. She believes the discovery of this deep connection between music and movement may cast light on why disabled patients can benefit from listening to music – and could also prove useful with other impairments such as those involved in sound production. 'It's been shown that people who talk with a stutter might have problems in this auditory-motor loop.'
 
I For researchers working in this new area of science, these early discoveries hold the promise of much more to come. Zatorre and his colleagues are investigating whether some people have more musical brains than others. 'We can see certain subtle brain features that can tell us how well somebody can do things like identify a slight change in a melody,' explains Zatorre. 'This ability could be enhanced by training – just like someone born with a predisposition to building strong muscles can enhance them by taking up weightlifting.'

questions.question: a reference to studies involving children

analyses.content: “Studies involving children” 对应 “tests, even three-year-olds”。
(Paragraph D) “In tests, even three-year-olds have been shown to link music in a major mode to happy faces...”
题目提到关于涉及儿童的研究的引用。原文D段末尾提到：“In tests, even three-year-olds have been shown to link music...（在测试中，甚至三岁的孩子也被证明会将音乐联系起来……）”，这是唯一提到儿童研究的地方，选 D。

questions.question: a mention of the discovery of significant artefacts

analyses.content: 题目提到重要文物发现的提及。原文B段提到考古学家发现了至少五万年前尼安德特人演奏的“musical instruments（乐器）”，这是典型的“significant artefacts（重要文物/人工制品）”，选 B。
“Significant artefacts” 对应 “musical instruments played by Neanderthals at least 50,000 years ago”。
(Paragraph B) “Given that archaeologists have found musical instruments played by Neanderthals...”

questions.question: reasons why a particular aspect of music has not been researched

analyses.content: 题目提到为什么音乐的某个特定方面没有被研究的原因。原文C段开头Norman Cook解释了为什么心理学家不愿触及这个话题：“there's an image problem in tackling the emotionality of music... Emotion is such a slippery topic（处理音乐的情感性存在形象问题……情感是一个棘手的话题）”，以及长期以来认为音乐反应是习得的原则，这解释了为什么之前没研究，选 C。
“Reasons why... not been researched” 对应 “image problem... slippery topic... long-standing principle”。
(Paragraph C) “...there's an image problem in tackling the emotionality of music... Emotion is such a slippery topic.”

questions.question: a mention of an unexpected discovery involving two different areas of the brain

analyses.content: “Unexpected discovery” 对应 “surprising... revelation”，“Two different areas” 对应 “parts... linked to hearing” 和 “motor regions”。
题目提到涉及大脑两个不同区域的意外发现。原文G段末尾提到研究结果是另一个启示（revelation），节奏不仅激活了与听觉相关的大脑部分（parts linked to hearing），更令人惊讶的是（even more surprising），还激活了大脑的运动区域（motor regions），即两个不同区域，选 G。
(Paragraph G) “...rhythms triggered activity in parts of the brain linked to hearing, but something even more surprising was that the rhythms also triggered activity in the motor regions...”

questions.question: a comparison of tone variations produced by certain animals and humans

analyses.content: 题目提到某些动物和人类产生的音调变化的比较。原文E段Cook指出同样的音高变化（same change in pitch）在某些哺乳动物的交流中起作用（rising communicate weakness...），这也存在于我们的语言中（present in our speech），构成了比较，选 E。
“Comparison... animals and humans” 对应 “communication between some mammals... also present in our speech”。
(Paragraph E) “The same change in pitch works... in communication between some mammals... It's also present in our speech.”

groups.contentHtml: A study involving collaboration between researchers in Oxford and Montreal. The participants in this study led by Dr Chen were chosen because they were not musicians, and they demonstrated a good state of . The participants were given while music with a very noticeable rhythm was being played. Previous research had indicated that listening to this type of music seemed to be of assistance to some people. By listening to it, their ability had definitely got better. The findings of Dr Chen's study proved most informative.

analyses.content: 题目说参与者表现出良好的____状态。原文G段提到选择志愿者的标准是他们应该处于一流的“physical health（身体健康）”但未受过音乐训练，填 physical health。
“Good state of” 对应 “first-rate”。
(Paragraph G) “...they should be in first-rate physical health but musically untrained.”
(Paragraph G) “...carried out brain scans on volunteers who were listening to rhythmic sounds.”
“Given ______” 对应 “carried out brain scans on”。
题目说参与者在播放节奏明显的音乐时接受了____。原文G段提到Chen博士和同事对正在听节奏声音的志愿者进行了“carried out brain scans（进行了脑部扫描）”，即给予了扫描，填 brain scans。
题目说这种音乐似乎对一些____人有帮助。原文G段提到之前的研究涉及有运动困难的病人，想找出为什么听音乐可能帮助“disabled patients（残疾病人）”，填 disabled。
“Assistance to some ______ people” 对应 “help disabled patients”。
(Paragraph G) “In an attempt to find out why... might help disabled patients...”
题目说通过听音乐，他们的____能力肯定变好了。原文G段提到如果播放强节奏音乐，病人能够改善他们的“walking ability（行走能力）”，填 walking。
“______ ability... got better” 对应 “improve their walking ability”。
(Paragraph G) “...they were able to improve their walking ability...”

questions.question: Research into the brain activity set off by music may help people with speech defects.

analyses.content: (Paragraph H) “...useful with other impairments... people who talk with a stutter... says Chen.”
题目说对音乐引发的大脑活动的研究可能帮助有语言缺陷的人。原文H段 Joyce Chen 提到这一发现可能对其他损伤有用，例如涉及发声的损伤，并具体指出“talk with a stutter（口吃）”的人可能在这个听觉-运动回路有问题，口吃属于语言缺陷，选 C。
“Speech defects” 对应 “stutter / sound production impairments”。

questions.question: It may be possible in time to improve a person's ability to recognise certain musical characteristics.

analyses.content: 题目说将来有可能提高一个人识别某些音乐特征的能力。原文I段 Robert Zatorre 说我们可以看到大脑特征告诉我们某人识别旋律微小变化（identify a slight change in a melody）的能力如何，并且这种能力“could be enhanced by training（可以通过训练增强）”，选 B。
“Improve... ability to recognise... characteristics” 对应 “enhanced by training... identify a slight change”。
(Paragraph I) “'This ability could be enhanced by training...' explains Zatorre.”

questions.question: The way listeners react to certain musical combinations may be similar to the way they react to other noises.

analyses.content: 题目说听众对某些音乐组合的反应方式可能与他们对其他噪音的反应方式相似。原文E段 Norman Cook 分析人们对音符的反应与大脑在日常生活中解释某些声音（interpret certain sounds in everyday life）有关，并对比了动物叫声和人类语音语调（noises/sounds），选 A。
“React to certain musical combinations... similar to... other noises” 对应 “respond to notes... link with... interpret certain sounds in everyday life / speech / animal communication”。
(Paragraph E) “According to Cook, analysis of how people respond to notes suggests a link with how our brains interpret certain sounds in everyday life.”

questions.question: When a person reacts positively to music, the same parts of the brain are stimulated as when certain animals react to a positive outcome.

analyses.content: 题目说当人对音乐产生积极反应时，受到刺激的大脑部分与某些动物对积极结果产生反应时的部分相同。原文F段 Robert Zatorre 说令人愉悦的音乐激活了大脑回路，“We share it with rats（我们与老鼠共享它）”且这通常与“biological rewards, like food（生物奖励，如食物/积极结果）”相关，选 B。
“Reacts positively” 对应 “pleasurable music”；“Same parts... animals react to a positive outcome” 对应 “share it with rats... associated with biological rewards”。
(Paragraph F) “'We share it with rats... associated with biological rewards, like food...' says Zatorre.”
